## Where to start

Open the **Issues** tab. There are eight of them, Gate 0 to Gate 7, and they are the
study in order. Each one explains what it means, why it matters, what to produce, and
what good looks like. Start at Gate 0 — it takes about five minutes and exists so the
GitHub mechanics are behind you before anything hard starts.

You do not need to install anything, and you never need the command line. Every file
these issues ask for can be created and edited in your browser.

## Your progress is tracked for you

Nobody will ask you for a status update, and you are never expected to move an issue
to report progress. When you commit the work a gate asks for, the gate issue moves to
*Ready for review* on its own and a comment appears saying what changed.

[**How this repository is tracked**](HOW-THIS-REPO-IS-TRACKED.md) explains exactly what
the automation does, what it deliberately does not do, and why things move without you
touching them. Worth five minutes if you would rather not be surprised.

## Quick access

- **Project board:** [Study board]({{PROJECT_URL}}) — three views: Milestones, Work items, Data partners
- **Programme tracking:** [Factory issue #{{FACTORY_ISSUE_NUMBER}}](https://github.com/{{FACTORY_REPO}}/issues/{{FACTORY_ISSUE_NUMBER}})

## Data partners

Add a row to [`partners.csv`](partners.csv) for each institution you approach, and a
tracking issue is created for it automatically. Keep each issue's body current, and add
a short comment after every exchange — what was asked, and what happens next.

Keep having your actual conversations by email and on calls. The issue is a log, not an
inbox.

## If you are stuck

Post in the study channel or bring it to office hours. Most of you have not used GitHub
before, and that is entirely normal — a clumsy first commit is exactly right. Asking is
always the right move.
